title: Adversus Arium
author: Marius Victorinus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp115.tmp115.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Illa quoque ex istorum refutatione vincamus. Et primum definiendas sunt Arii Eusebii- que sententias, in quo nobis consentiant, in quibus discrepent, in quibus ipsi sibi videantur adversi. Arius ait, quoniam filius non est ingenitus. Item Eusebius, hoc idem quod duo non sint ingenita. Nobis quoque ista sententia est. Arius, filius, inquit, pars ingeniti non est, neque est ex aliquo subjecto : haec duo et Eu- sebius.
passages.english: Let us also overcome those [points] by refuting these men. And first the opinions of Arius and Eusebius must be set out: in what they agree with us, in what they differ, and in what they seem opposed to themselves. Arius says that the Son is not unbegotten. Likewise Eusebius [says] this same thing, that there are not two unbegotten [beings]. This opinion is ours too. Arius says, "The Son is not a part of the unbegotten, nor is he from any underlying substrate": these two [points] Eusebius [holds] too.
passages.notes: "definiendas sunt ... sententias" is ungrammatical (probably for "definiendae sunt ... sententiae"); translated in that sense. "ex aliquo subjecto" renders the Greek idea of "from any substrate" (ex hypokeimenou).

passages.original: Jam vero ex non subjecto esse ferre non possumus : non quod nos ex aliquo sub- jecto esse dicamus, sed quod a patre ut filium. Arius, voluntate, inquit. Dei subsistit filuis ante tem- pora et aeones. Idem et Eusebius : Nos ante omnes aeones, et ante omnia tempora; sed genitum dici- mus, non factum, non creatum, non fundatum. Arius dicit : Filium factum, scilicet plenum Deum, unigenitum, immutabilem, qui antequam crearetur non fuerit, propterea quod non sit ingenitus.
passages.english: Now, that [the Son] is from what is not a subject, we cannot accept; not because we say that he is from some subject, but because [we say he is] from the Father as Son. Arius says: "By [the Father's] will the Son of God subsists before times and ages." Eusebius says the same: "We [say he is] before all ages and before all times; but we say he was begotten, not made, not created, not founded." Arius says: "The Son was made, that is, full God, only-begotten, unchangeable, who before he was created did not exist, because he is not unbegotten."
passages.notes: "Nos ante omnes aeones...": the text attributes this to Eusebius, but the phrasing "genitum dicimus, non factum" sounds like the orthodox position, so the attribution or punctuation may be confused. "filuis" is read as "filius". "ex non subjecto" is a difficult phrase and probably answers the Arian claim that the Son is "not from any subject"; the sense is uncertain.

passages.original: Tu autem scribis ista et dicis : quae Samosatenus Paulos, et Marcellus, et Photinus, et nunc Valens et Ursacius, et alii istius modi in hae- resi religiosi inventi destructi sunt. Numquid omoov dicentes? Non. Quomodo autem blasphemantes? Sa- mosatenus sicuti Arius : ex nihilo, et quod fuit quan- do non fuit, quod factura filius, et omnino omnimo- dis dissimilis patri. Quid Marcellus et Photinus? Tantam hominem ex homine Jesum, et esse Triadem extra Jesum. Et nunc Valens et Ursacius reliquiae Arii.
passages.english: But you write and say these things: that Paul of Samosata, and Marcellus, and Photinus, and now Valens and Ursacius, and others of that kind, having been found [to be] devotees in heresy, were brought down. Was it for saying homoousios? No. How, then? For blaspheming. Paul of Samosata [said], just as Arius [does]: [that the Son is] from nothing, and that there was when he was not, that the Son is a thing made, and altogether in every way unlike the Father. What [did] Marcellus and Photinus [say]? That Jesus was only a man from a man, and that the Trinity exists apart from Jesus. And now Valens and Ursacius are the remnants of Arius.
passages.notes: "omoov" is a garbled "homoousion" (cf. context after). "in haeresi religiosi" is odd and possibly corrupt; rendered literally. "Tantam" read as "tantum" (only). The punctuation of "Quomodo autem blasphemantes?" is uncertain; it may be one question: "How, then, [were they] blaspheming?"

passages.original: Etsi col- lisio facta est, fuit quando non fuit; et si compulsum faciendi et generatione factus est filius, praeexstitit factio et generatio antequam fuisset filius. Posteriora nutem ista. Quomodo ergo compulsio? Et hoc Arii : deinde quomodo ista collisio? et quorum et in quo? Numquid voluntatum in Deo concursio? Numquid pas- sionum aut differentiarum, maxime contrariarum mo- tionum? Et si istud passus est pater, qui est sine pas- sione, et non ex sua substantia apparuit ei filius : colli- sione enim duarum aut voluntatum, aut passionum, nec voluntas facta est, nec passio, multo magis nec substantia a substantia paterna, sed extra quaedam substantia, quae ex nihilo existeret de λόγω ad patrem.
passages.english: Even if a collision took place, there was [a time] when he was not; and if the Son was made by a striking-together of making and generation, the making and the generation existed before the Son had existed. But these are later [than him]. How, then, a striking-together? This too is Arius's [teaching]. Next, how [could there be] this collision? Both of what things, and in what? Is it a clash of wills in God? Is it [a clash] of passions or of differences, above all of contrary motions? And if the Father, who is without passion, underwent this, then the Son did not appear to him out of his own substance: for by the collision of two wills or passions there came to be neither a will nor a passion, much less a substance from the paternal substance, but some substance outside [it], which would exist out of nothing, from the Word to the Father.
passages.notes: "nutem" read as "autem". The final phrase "de λόγω ad patrem" is obscure and possibly corrupt; rendered literally. The passage as a whole is a clumsy Latin, apparently translated from Greek, and several constructions are uncertain.

passages.original: etiam ratione admodum verum est : certe Deus, cui ad omnipotentiam priu- cipalemque summitatem hoc nomen convenit Deus : Deus, inquam, primum, si in Dei operibus dicendum aliquid primum : sed intelligentia humani ingenii, ut se excrat et res capiat, rebus vel simul existentibus, vel simul fusis; et ortus, et diversos ortus,et quasi tempus attribuit. Deus, inquam, primo universalium existentias substantiasque progenuit : has Plato ideas Vocat; cunctarum inexistentibus specierum species principales; quod genus in exemplo est όντότuc, ζωότης, vbijotc : Et item τουτότης et τϊρότης (1), atque hoc genus caetera : genera igitur generum profundun- tur, adeo omnium potentiarum potentias universaliter principales.
passages.english: It is also quite true by reason: certainly God, to whom this name "God" belongs by reason of his omnipotence and sovereign supremacy; God, I say, [is] first, if anything is to be called first among the works of God. But the understanding of the human mind, in order to exert itself and grasp things, assigns to things which either exist together or have flowed forth together both an origin, and different origins, and as it were a time. God, I say, first begot the existences and substances of universals: these Plato calls ideas, the principal species of all the species existing in [things]; of which kind, for example, are ontotēs [beingness], zōotēs [lifeness], nootēs [mindness]; and likewise tautotēs [sameness] and heterotēs [otherness], and the rest of this kind. So the genera of genera are poured forth, and thus the universally principal potencies of all potencies.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled in the scan: "όντότuc, ζωότης, vbijotc" is read as ontotēs, zōotēs, nootēs, and "τουτότης et τϊρότης" as tautotēs and heterotēs; these readings are conjectural. "excrat" is read as "exerat" or "exerceat", and "priu- cipalemque" as "principalemque". The sentence begins mid-thought, continuing "Hoc cum rectum;" from the context before. The syntax of "Deus, inquam, primum" is elliptical.
